name: Portfolio Optimisation Beyond Mean and Variance
title: Portfolio Optimisation Beyond Mean and Variance
answer: Portfolio optimisation beyond mean and variance covers the methods used to choose asset weights when return and risk are not fully described by an average and a standard deviation. It includes downside risk measures such as value at risk and expected shortfall, higher moment objectives such as skewness and kurtosis, drawdown control, and multi period or path dependent formulations. The scope also takes in robust and distributionally robust versions, where the investor hedges against uncertainty in the estimated inputs rather than trusting a single forecast. It sits inside portfolio construction and draws on statistics, optimisation and, increasingly, machine learning for estimation and for solving the resulting problems.

sections.body: Portfolio optimisation beyond mean and variance covers the methods used to choose asset weights when return and risk are not fully described by an average and a standard deviation. It includes downside risk measures such as value at risk and expected shortfall, higher moment objectives such as skewness and kurtosis, drawdown control, and multi period or path dependent formulations. The scope also takes in robust and distributionally robust versions, where the investor hedges against uncertainty in the estimated inputs rather than trusting a single forecast. It sits inside portfolio construction and draws on statistics, optimisation and, increasingly, machine learning for estimation and for solving the resulting problems.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on standard numerical computing: Python with libraries such as NumPy, pandas and SciPy, and optimisation solvers for convex and mixed integer problems. Scenario based methods need large simulated or historical return paths, so storage and compute scale with the number of scenarios and assets. Machine learning components, for example generative models for scenarios or neural networks for conditional risk, usually run on GPU hardware. Data feeds cover prices, fundamentals, factor exposures and, for some methods, option implied distributions. Results are typically held in a research pipeline that feeds an order management or portfolio accounting system.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical study starts by defining the objective, for example minimising expected shortfall subject to a return target, then estimating the inputs from historical or simulated data. Because higher moment and tail objectives are often non convex, practitioners use scenario approximation, convex relaxations or heuristic search, and they check stability with rolling or walk forward backtests. Estimation error is handled by shrinkage, factor models, resampling or robust formulations that treat the inputs as uncertain within a set. Machine learning enters mainly at the estimation stage, for instance predicting conditional volatility or generating scenarios, and the optimiser is then run on those outputs. Results are compared against simpler mean variance portfolios to see whether the added complexity earns its keep.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: These methods carry model risk because tail and higher moment estimates are sensitive to the sample and to the assumptions behind any simulation. Documentation should record the objective, the constraints, the data window, the solver and the fallback rules used when the optimiser fails or returns an unstable solution. Where machine learning supplies forecasts, versioning of models and training data matters for reproducibility and for audit. Regulatory and internal limits on leverage, concentration and liquidity still apply, and a tail risk objective does not remove the need to test portfolios against stressed markets. Nothing here is legal, financial or investment advice, and any live use should follow the firm's own risk and compliance process.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Research is moving toward objectives that combine several risk measures, toward distributionally robust formulations with tractable convex forms, and toward end to end learning where allocation is trained directly rather than solved in two stages. Scenario generation with generative models is an active area, as is the use of reinforcement learning for multi period problems with transaction costs and constraints. Practitioners are also paying more attention to explainability and to stress testing, since complex objectives are harder to justify to a committee. The likely direction is not replacement of mean variance but a layered approach, where simple models set the baseline and richer methods are adopted only where they show consistent out of sample benefit.
